tightcut: Equality at k says the k lowest diagonals add up to −k(n−k), the smallest total possible for k points in different rows and columns; that minimum forces those k points into the bottom k rows and the leftmost k columns. So D splits into the lower k stones (shifted up by n−k) and the upper n−k stones (shifted down by k). Both shifted sets inherit Landau's inequalities from the prefix sums, with equality at their own sizes, so they are valid smaller instances. Put a witness of the first in the bottom-left k×k block and a witness of the second in the top-right block: the shifts put every point back on its original diagonal.
fixedpoint: Put a point at (1,1); it is on diagonal 0 and uses row 1 and column 1. Deleting them leaves rows and columns 2…n, and every remaining cell keeps its diagonal. So a witness of D∖{0} at size n−1, shifted down and right by one, fills the rest.
directsum: Place π₁ in the top-left n₁×n₁ block and π₂ in the bottom-right block. Each point keeps its diagonal (both blocks sit on the main diagonal), rows and columns are disjoint between the blocks, and the diagonals don't collide because D₁ ∩ D₂ = ∅.
pn: Odd positions i ≤ n−2 get the values n−1−i and even positions i ≥ 4 get n+3−i: two staircases using opposite parity classes of values, so together with n (at position 2) and the leftover value they form a permutation. Diagonals: n−2 at i = 2, 2−n at the leftover position, n−1−2i at odd i and n−1−2(i−2) at even i ≥ 4. The last two together give every n−1−2r for 1 ≤ r ≤ n−2, i.e. {n−3, n−5, …, 3−n}, which is the rest of P_n.
f1: Rows i ≤ a go to column 2i, so diagonal 2i − i = i takes the values 1…a on the even columns 2, 4, …, 2a. Rows i > a go to column 2i − 2a − 1, so diagonal i − 2a − 1 takes the values −a…−1 on the odd columns 1, 3, …, 2a − 1. All columns are distinct, so this is a permutation using each diagonal ±1…±a once.
f3: An involution's 2-cycles i ↔ j give the points (i, j) and (j, i), on diagonals +(j − i) and −(j − i). So an involution witness for ±L is the same thing as a pairing of the positions with distances exactly L, and a fixed point adds diagonal 0. Skolem (1957) shows {1…2m} pairs with distances {1…m} iff m ≡ 0, 1 (mod 4); Simpson (1983) settles distances {d…d+m−1}, and Shalaby's near-Skolem theorem settles {1…k} ∖ {m} on positions 1…2k−2.
mm: Induct on the number of 3-cycles. A non-transitive valid D has two equal scores; take a maximal run of equal scores v and undo a move at its two ends (v, v → v−1, v+1). The result stays sorted, its prefix sums drop by 1 only inside the run, and none of those prefixes can be tight (a tight prefix at k forces s_k < s_{k+1}), so it is still valid with one fewer 3-cycle. Each forward move only raises prefix sums, so it keeps Landau.
ly: Li–Yao / Li–Liu–Yao: by LP duality, a doubly stochastic matrix with these diagonal sums exists iff a family of weighted inequalities I(w) holds for all weights w ≥ 0; an induction on the weights reduces every I(w) to Landau's finitely many inequalities.
inflation: Let π_i be a witness of G_i − c_i (size n_i). Give block i the rows after the groups that precede it in the row order, and the columns after the groups that precede it in the column order; by hypothesis, column start − row start = c_i. A point of π_i at local position (r, c) lands at (row start + r, column start + c), so its diagonal is its local diagonal plus c_i, which lies in G_i. Blocks use disjoint rows and disjoint columns, so the result is a permutation, and since the groups partition D, every diagonal of D is used exactly once.
interface: Number rows from the bottom, r′ = n+1−r. A point on diagonal d = c − r has r′ + c = d + n + 1, so the k-th smallest diagonal needs r′ + c = b_k := d_k + n + 1 = 2k + e_k. A witness is a pair of bijections ρ, γ: {1…n} → {1…n} with ρ(k) + γ(k) = b_k. Let R_k = ρ({1…k}), C_k = γ({1…k}), and for a k-set X let exc(X) = ΣX − k(k+1)/2 ≥ 0. Then exc(R_k) + exc(C_k) = Σ_{i≤k} b_i − k(k+1) = σ_k. A k-set X = {x_1 < … < x_k} with excess j is the partition of j with parts x_i − i, so (R_k, C_k) is a pair of partitions with σ_k boxes in total; it starts and ends empty. Step k adds row k + u and column k + v with u + v = e_k, and whether a row or column is free depends only on the partitions and on u, v, not on k or n (n only enters through 'row ≤ n', which holds automatically because the final excess is 0). Conversely any such sequence of sets gives ρ and γ. If σ_k ≤ B then each excess is ≤ B, so a k-set contains {1…k−B} and is contained in {1…k+B}: finitely many states, and the transition rule is the same for all k.
